fixture.goal: Wants to feel more natural and less rehearsed in conversation.

fixture.emotionalSignal: accepts the idea but is raising a real, specific objection — he's engaged, not resistant; the 'however' is a genuine obstacle he wants solved, not dismissed
fixture.expectedCoachMove: Take the 'however' seriously — validate the specific obstacle (pausing feels like losing your place) and adapt the advice rather than repeating it. Reframe the pause so it has a job (pick the ONE next word during the beat), which solves the lost-train-of-thought problem instead of waving it away. Warm register: curious, with him in it.
fixture.badAnswerExample: Just keep practicing the pause and it'll get more natural over time. Pauses are important for authority. You've got this — try to be more confident with the silence.
fixture.excellentAnswerExample: That's the real catch, yeah — an empty pause does feel like a cliff. So give it a job: in that one beat, don't go blank, just pick the single next word you're heading for. The silence stops being 'lost' and starts being you choosing. Try it on one sentence next rep, not the whole thing.

Then, lightly, anchor to evidence that the capacity is already there (held composure through an interruption this week) so the encouragement is earned, not hollow. fixture.goal: Reduce filler words, especially when put on the spot.

fixture.emotionalSignal: practical, a bit self-critical — genuinely wants a mechanism, not comfort
fixture.expectedCoachMove: Reframe fillers as a timing reflex, not a vocabulary problem — coach the PAUSE as the replacement (hold a silent beat instead of filling). Cite his own split (3 calm vs 9 under pressure) so it's diagnostic. One concrete move: the silent-beat swap. Must coach the pause, NOT tell him to close his mouth/lips or 'stop saying um'. Frame as a test.
fixture.badAnswerExample: Just slow down and think before you speak. Close your mouth when you feel an um coming. Practice more and be more confident — the ums will naturally go away once you work on your confidence.
fixture.excellentAnswerExample: That spike is timing, not vocabulary — calm you sits at 3 fillers; put on the spot you hit 9. The um is you starting the sentence before you know the end of it. So swap the um for a silent beat: when the question lands, hold one second, pick your first word, then go. Try it next Sudden Death rep — one held beat before each answer. That tests whether the pause can do the job the um was doing.

fixture.goal: Wants to end statements with conviction instead of trailing off or upspeaking.

fixture.expectedCoachMove: Name the specific mechanism from the STRUCTURE READ: he lands the point then keeps going, adding a trailing softener with rising pitch. The fix is to STOP on the strong sentence — end the sentence as the point and hold the silence, don't fill it. One concrete move (make the last sentence the ask, then stop; no 'so yeah'). fixture.badAnswerExample: Work on your confidence and projection! Practice ending sentences with a downward inflection. Record yourself and listen back. The more you practice, the more natural your strong endings will become. Believe in what you're saying!

Next rep: end on the point, resist the 'so yeah,' let it sit.
